claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is amenable to studying membrane traffic by live-cell fluorescence microscopy.
source: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is amenable to studying membrane traffic by live-cell fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of S. cerevisiae for microscopy studies, supported by the established use of this system in the field.

claim: A biosynthetic vacuolar cargo was modified by adding a vacuolar targeting signal to a regulatable fluorescent secretory cargo.
source: To address this question, we modified a regulatable fluorescent secretory cargo by adding a vacuolar targeting signal.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and construction of the vacuolar cargo.

claim: Traffic of the vacuolar cargo requires the GGA clathrin adaptors.
source: Traffic of the vacuolar cargo requires the GGA clathrin adaptors, which arrive during the early-to-late Golgi transition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of GGAs prevents normal cargo sorting.

claim: GGA clathrin adaptors arrive during the early-to-late Golgi transition.
source: Traffic of the vacuolar cargo requires the GGA clathrin adaptors, which arrive during the early-to-late Golgi transition.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis showing GGA arrival timing relative to Golgi maturation markers.

claim: The vacuolar cargo begins to exit the Golgi near the midpoint of maturation, significantly before exit of a secretory cargo.
source: Accordingly, the vacuolar cargo begins to exit the Golgi near the midpoint of maturation, significantly before exit of a secretory cargo.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data tracking cargo through Golgi maturation.

claim: Stable PVE compartments repeatedly deliver material to the vacuole by a kiss-and-run mechanism.
source: The results suggest that stable PVE compartments repeatedly deliver material to the vacuole by a kiss-and-run mechanism.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations showing gradual and burst-like transfer of cargo from PVE compartments to vacuoles without complete fusion.

claim: Genetic screens of Saccharomyces cerevisiae have identified many conserved components of the biosynthetic and endocytic machineries.
source: Genetic screens of Saccharomyces cerevisiae have identified many conserved components of the biosynthetic and endocytic machineries (Kaiser et al., 1997; Novick et al., 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior genetic screen studies.

claim: 4D fluorescence microscopy of S. cerevisiae has been powerful for characterizing membrane traffic pathways.
source: In addition, 4D (time-lapse 3D) fluorescence microscopy of S. cerevisiae has been powerful for characterizing membrane traffic pathways (Day et al., 2016; Kurokawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior microscopy studies.

claim: S. cerevisiae has a non-stacked Golgi in which individual cisternae are optically resolvable by fluorescence microscopy.
source: Unlike most eukaryotes, S. cerevisiae has a non-stacked Golgi in which individual cisternae are optically resolvable by fluorescence microscopy (Preuss et al., 1992; Wooding and Pelham, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies and is established knowledge about yeast Golgi architecture.

claim: The non-stacked Golgi property enabled the first direct visualization of Golgi cisternal maturation.
source: This property enabled the first direct visualization of Golgi cisternal maturation (Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006) as well as later studies of how maturation is regulated by GTPases and vesicle coat proteins (Ishii et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2016; Papanikou et al., 2015; Rivera-Molina and Novick, 2009; Suda et al., 2013; Thomas and Fromme, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original studies that visualized cisternal maturation.

claim: New Golgi cisternae arise at ER exit sites and capture biosynthetic cargoes from the ER.
source: New Golgi cisternae arise at ER exit sites and capture biosynthetic cargoes from the ER.
evidence: This is part of the established model of Golgi maturation cited in the manuscript.

claim: Golgi cisternae mature by recycling resident Golgi proteins to the ER and to younger cisternae.
source: These cisternae then mature by recycling resident Golgi proteins to the ER and to younger cisternae.
evidence: This is part of the established model of Golgi maturation.

claim: During the early stage of maturation, one set of resident Golgi membrane proteins recycles with the aid of the COPI vesicle coat.
source: During the early stage of maturation, one set of resident Golgi membrane proteins recycles with the aid of the COPI vesicle coat, whereas during the late stage of maturation, another set of resident Golgi membrane proteins recycles with the aid of the AP-1 clathrin adaptor.
evidence: This is part of the established model of Golgi maturation.

claim: During the late stage of maturation, another set of resident Golgi membrane proteins recycles with the aid of the AP-1 clathrin adaptor.
source: During the early stage of maturation, one set of resident Golgi membrane proteins recycles with the aid of the COPI vesicle coat, whereas during the late stage of maturation, another set of resident Golgi membrane proteins recycles with the aid of the AP-1 clathrin adaptor.
evidence: This is part of the established model of Golgi maturation.

claim: Biosynthetic cargoes are present in the cisternae throughout the maturation process.
source: Biosynthetic cargoes are present in the cisternae throughout the maturation process (Casler et al., 2019; Kurokawa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Terminally mature Golgi cisternae fragment into secretory vesicles.
source: Finally, the terminally mature Golgi cisternae fragment into secretory vesicles.
evidence: This is part of the established model of Golgi maturation.

claim: S. cerevisiae has a minimal endomembrane system in which the late Golgi (TGN) plays an additional role as an early and recycling endosome.
source: The evidence indicates that S. cerevisiae has a minimal endomembrane system in which the late Golgi, also known as the trans-Golgi network (TGN), plays an additional role as an early and recycling endosome (Day et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Yeast cells have two types of endosomes: the late Golgi/TGN, and PVE compartments that are typically attached to the vacuole.
source: According to this view, yeast cells have two types of endosomes: (a) the late Golgi/TGN, and (b) PVE compartments that are typically attached to the vacuole.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The tetrapeptide QRPL from the CPY propeptide is necessary and sufficient to direct CPY from the Golgi to PVE compartments by means of the Vps10 cargo receptor.
source: Prior studies showed that within the propeptide, the tetrapeptide QRPL is necessary and sufficient to direct CPY from the Golgi to PVE compartments by means of the sorting receptor Vps10 (Johnson et al., 1987; Marcusson et al., 1994; Valls et al., 1987; Valls et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Vps10 is packaged into clathrin-coated vesicles destined for PVE compartments with the aid of the GGA adaptors Gga1 and Gga2.
source: This targeting signal is recognized in the Golgi by the Vps10 cargo receptor (Marcusson et al., 1994), which in turn is packaged, with the aid of the GGA adaptors Gga1 and Gga2, into clathrin-coated vesicles destined for PVE compartments (reviewed in Myers and Payne, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some vacuolar membrane proteins traffic directly from the Golgi to the vacuole with the aid of the Golgi-associated AP-3 adaptor complex.
source: Some vacuolar membrane proteins traffic directly from the Golgi to the vacuole with the aid of the Golgi-associated AP-3 adaptor complex (Cowles et al., 1997; Llinares et al., 2015; Odorizzi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CPY and certain other vacuolar hydrolases first traffic from the Golgi to PVE compartments.
source: By contrast, CPY and certain other vacuolar hydrolases first traffic from the Golgi to PVE compartments (Conibear and Stevens, 1998; Vida et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: PVE compartments contain endocytosed cargoes, such as the methionine permease Mup1, that are in transit to the vacuole.
source: The same PVE compartments also contain endocytosed cargoes, such as the methionine permease Mup1, that are in transit to the vacuole (Menant et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Within PVE compartments, transmembrane cargo proteins such as Mup1 are packaged into intraluminal vesicles that are transferred from the PVE compartments to the vacuole, where the intraluminal vesicles are degraded.
source: Within PVE compartments, transmembrane cargo proteins such as Mup1 are packaged into intraluminal vesicles that are transferred from the PVE compartments to the vacuole, where the intraluminal vesicles are degraded (MacDonald et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: GGAs arrive earlier than AP-1 and at about the same time as Sec7.
source: We have now replicated work from the Payne lab showing that GGAs arrive earlier than AP-1 and at about the same time as Sec7 (Daboussi et al., 2012), an Arf guanine nucleotide exchange factor that is recruited and activated during the early-to-late Golgi transition (Losev et al., 2006; McDonold and Fromme, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and the authors' replication of those findings.

claim: Sec7 is an Arf guanine nucleotide exchange factor that is recruited and activated during the early-to-late Golgi transition.
source: We have now replicated work from the Payne lab showing that GGAs arrive earlier than AP-1 and at about the same time as Sec7 (Daboussi et al., 2012), an Arf guanine nucleotide exchange factor that is recruited and activated during the early-to-late Golgi transition (Losev et al., 2006; McDonold and Fromme, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The late/TGN stage of Golgi maturation can be divided into a first sub-stage marked by the exit of vacuolar cargoes to PVE compartments, followed by a second sub-stage marked by AP-1-dependent intra-Golgi recycling and by the exit of secretory cargoes to the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, the late/TGN stage of Golgi maturation can be divided into a first sub-stage marked by the exit of vacuolar cargoes to PVE compartments, followed by a second sub-stage marked by AP-1-dependent intra-Golgi recycling and by the exit of secretory cargoes to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: It was assumed that in yeast, early endosomes would mature into PVE compartments that would be consumed by fusing with the vacuole.
source: By analogy to mammalian cells, it was assumed that in yeast, early endosomes would mature into PVE compartments that would be consumed by fusing with the vacuole (Balderhaar and Ungermann, 2013; Feyder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of a prior assumption in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Maturation of PVE compartments has not been observed.
source: Yet maturation of PVE compartments has not been observed—and indeed, if we are correct that yeast cells lack distinct early endosomes, then maturation of yeast endosomes is logically precluded (Day et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on the authors' observations and prior work.

claim: If yeast cells lack distinct early endosomes, then maturation of yeast endosomes is logically precluded.
source: Yet maturation of PVE compartments has not been observed—and indeed, if we are correct that yeast cells lack distinct early endosomes, then maturation of yeast endosomes is logically precluded (Day et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the proposed model.

claim: PVE compartments are stable organelles.
source: The implication is that PVE compartments are not continually regenerated and must therefore be stable organelles.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that PVE compartments do not mature.

claim: PVE compartments undergo fission and homotypic fusion but otherwise persist indefinitely.
source: In support of this concept, our previous live-cell imaging revealed that PVE compartments undergo fission and homotypic fusion but otherwise persist indefinitely (Day et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The regulatable secretory cargo consists of the tetrameric red fluorescent protein DsRed-Express2 fused to a dimerizing variant of FKBP, with a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence to direct cotranslational translocation into the ER.
source: Our secretory cargo consists of the tetrameric red fluorescent protein DsRed-Express2 fused to a dimerizing variant of FKBP, with a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence to direct cotranslational translocation into the ER.
evidence: This describes the construction of the cargo protein used in the study.

claim: The signal sequence is followed by a tripeptide ER export signal and a signal for N-linked glycosylation.
source: The signal sequence is followed by a tripeptide ER export signal (Yin et al., 2018) and a signal for N-linked glycosylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the construction of the cargo protein, with reference to a figure and a citation.

claim: The fusion protein forms fluorescent aggregates within the ER lumen, and the aggregates can be dissolved by adding a synthetic ligand of FKBP (SLF) that blocks dimerization of FKBP.
source: This fusion protein forms fluorescent aggregates within the ER lumen, and the aggregates can be dissolved by adding a synthetic ligand of FKBP (SLF) that blocks dimerization of FKBP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the regulatable cargo system, with reference to a figure.

claim: Efficient dissolution of the aggregates requires a drug-sensitive yeast strain.
source: Efficient dissolution of the aggregates requires a drug-sensitive yeast strain.
evidence: This is a technical requirement for the experimental system.

claim: All experiments with the regulatable cargoes employed yeast strains containing deletions of the transcription factors Pdr1 and Pdr3, which mediate pleiotropic drug resistance.
source: Thus, all of our experiments with the regulatable cargoes employed yeast strains containing deletions of the transcription factors Pdr1 and Pdr3, which mediate pleiotropic drug resistance (Barrero et al., 2016; Casler et al., 2019; Coorey et al., 2015; Schüller et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the genetic background of the strains used, with citations to prior work.

claim: The regulatable secretory cargo persists in cisternae through the early-to-late transition of Golgi maturation.
source: We found previously that the regulatable secretory cargo persists in cisternae through the early-to-late transition of Golgi maturation, and that a fraction of the cargo molecules are recycled within the Golgi in an AP-1-dependent manner (Casler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A fraction of the secretory cargo molecules are recycled within the Golgi in an AP-1-dependent manner.
source: We found previously that the regulatable secretory cargo persists in cisternae through the early-to-late transition of Golgi maturation, and that a fraction of the cargo molecules are recycled within the Golgi in an AP-1-dependent manner (Casler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The vacuolar cargo was created by appending the peptide GSQRPLGGS at the C-terminus of the fusion protein.
source: We flanked QRPL with glycine/serine spacers by appending at the C-terminus of the fusion protein the peptide GSQRPLGGS (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the construction of the vacuolar cargo, with reference to a figure.

claim: Addition of the QRPL-containing peptide at the C-terminus preserved the formation of aggregates within the lumen of the ER.
source: Addition of the QRPL-containing peptide at the C-terminus preserved the formation of aggregates within the lumen of the ER, which was marked by GFP-tagged Erg11 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Some cargo molecules were already present in the vacuole prior to dissolution of the aggregates, presumably because signal-dependent ER exit allowed a fraction of the cargo molecules to escape from the ER and reach the vacuole while others became trapped in ER-localized aggregates.
source: Some cargo molecules were already present in the vacuole prior to dissolution of the aggregates (arrows in Figure 1C), presumably because signal-dependent ER exit allowed a fraction of the cargo molecules to escape from the ER and reach the vacuole while others became trapped in ER-localized aggregates (Casler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data with an interpretation based on prior work.

claim: The non-aggregating vacuolar cargo accumulated at high levels in the vacuole in a Vps10-dependent manner.
source: Compared to the non-aggregating secretory cargo, which accumulated at low levels in the vacuole (Casler et al., 2019), the non-aggregating vacuolar cargo accumulated at high levels in the vacuole in a Vps10-dependent manner (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: At 30 min after addition of SLF, the regulatable secretory cargo was detected in the culture medium whereas the regulatable vacuolar cargo was not.
source: At 30 min after addition of SLF, the regulatable secretory cargo was detected in the culture medium whereas the regulatable vacuolar cargo was not (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In typical VPS10 cells, small amounts of the cargo were detected in the vacuole within 8–15 min after SLF addition, and full delivery to the vacuole required at least 40 min.
source: In typical VPS10 cells, small amounts of the cargo were detected in the vacuole within 8–15 min after SLF addition, and full delivery to the vacuole required at least 40 min (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: About 35% of the cells required more than 15 min—and in some cases, more than 25 min—before any cargo appeared in the vacuole.
source: About 35% of the cells required more than 15 min—and in some cases, more than 25 min—before any cargo appeared in the vacuole (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: On average, the cell population showed a gradual increase in vacuolar fluorescence over a time course of an hour.
source: On average, the cell population showed a gradual increase in vacuolar fluorescence over a time course of an hour (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Following SLF addition, untreated and cycloheximide-treated cells showed similar traffic kinetics, with cycloheximide causing only a modest reduction in the amount of cargo accumulating in the vacuole.
source: Following SLF addition, untreated and cycloheximide-treated cells showed similar traffic kinetics, with cycloheximide causing only a modest reduction in the amount of cargo accumulating in the vacuole even though cell growth was arrested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinetics observed in the absence of cycloheximide reflect traffic of the vacuolar cargo molecules that were originally in ER-localized aggregates.
source: We conclude that to a close approximation, the kinetics observed in the absence of cycloheximide reflect traffic of the vacuolar cargo molecules that were originally in ER-localized aggregates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cycloheximide experiment.

claim: Secretory cargo molecules can travel from the ER to the plasma membrane within 5–10 min, and nearly all of them are secreted within 20 min.
source: For comparison, secretory cargo molecules can travel from the ER to the plasma membrane within 5–10 min, and nearly all of them are secreted within 20 min (Casler et al., 2019; Losev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In the absence of a sorting receptor, the vacuolar cargo behaves like a secretory cargo.
source: This effect is seen in the vps10∆ cells because in the absence of a sorting receptor, the vacuolar cargo behaves like a secretory cargo (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tagged Vps8 colocalized strongly with a variety of other PVE compartment markers.
source: We showed previously that tagged Vps8 colocalized strongly with a variety of other PVE compartment markers, and that the observed dynamics of PVE compartments were similar when using either tagged Vps8 or other markers (Day et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The observed dynamics of PVE compartments were similar when using either tagged Vps8 or other markers.
source: We showed previously that tagged Vps8 colocalized strongly with a variety of other PVE compartment markers, and that the observed dynamics of PVE compartments were similar when using either tagged Vps8 or other markers (Day et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Cargo accumulation within Golgi compartments occurred 1–5 min after SLF addition, followed by nearly complete transfer of the cargo to PVE compartments by 10 min.
source: The results showed cargo accumulation within Golgi compartments 1–5 min after SLF addition, followed by nearly complete transfer of the cargo to PVE compartments by 10 min (Figure 3—video 1 and Figure 3—video 2 and Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and associated videos.

claim: After 10 min, puncta that contained the cargo invariably labeled with Vps8-GFP, confirming that Vps8 is a reliable marker for PVE compartments.
source: After 10 min, puncta that contained the cargo invariably labeled with Vps8-GFP, confirming that Vps8 is a reliable marker for PVE compartments.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data that validates the use of Vps8 as a marker.

claim: The cargo gradually exited the PVE compartments and then accumulated in the vacuole.
source: The cargo gradually exited the PVE compartments and then accumulated in the vacuole as described above.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: Some PVE compartments did not immediately begin to transfer cargo to the vacuole, suggesting that PVE compartments can be temporarily quiescent with regard to cargo delivery.
source: Interestingly, even though the PVE compartments contained cargo by 10 min, some of them did not immediately begin to transfer cargo to the vacuole (see Figure 2B,D), suggesting that PVE compartments can be temporarily quiescent with regard to cargo delivery.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data with an interpretation.

claim: The rate-limiting step in traffic to the vacuole is not movement through the Golgi, but rather transfer of the cargo from PVE compartments to the vacuole.
source: These results verify that the rate-limiting step in traffic to the vacuole is not movement through the Golgi, but rather transfer of the cargo from PVE compartments to the vacuole.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis of cargo traffic.

claim: Although most of the early Golgi cisternae contained detectable vacuolar cargo at early time points, only about half of the late Golgi cisternae ever contained detectable vacuolar cargo.
source: Interestingly, although most of the early Golgi cisternae contained detectable vacuolar cargo at early time points, only about half of the late Golgi cisternae ever contained detectable vacuolar cargo (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The fluorescent secretory cargo was present in nearly all of the late Golgi cisternae, where it persisted until the final phase of maturation.
source: By contrast, we previously saw that the fluorescent secretory cargo was present in nearly all of the late Golgi cisternae, where it persisted until the final phase of maturation (Casler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The vacuolar cargo departed during the late stage of Golgi maturation, so that as late Golgi cisternae became more mature, they no longer contained fluorescent cargo.
source: A possible explanation is that the vacuolar cargo departed during the late stage of Golgi maturation, so that as late Golgi cisternae became more mature, they no longer contained fluorescent cargo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observation.

claim: The vacuolar cargo signal always began to decline near the midpoint of maturation.
source: Intriguingly, the vacuolar cargo signal always began to decline near the midpoint of maturation (Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4A,B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4 and associated videos.

claim: The rate of decline of the vacuolar cargo signal varied between cells, and the decline was slower in cells expressing very high levels of the vacuolar cargo, probably because the sorting machinery was saturated.
source: The rate of decline varied between cells, and qualitative observations indicated that the decline was slower in cells expressing very high levels of the vacuolar cargo (data not shown), probably because the sorting machinery was saturated.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data with an interpretation.

claim: In the absence of Vps10, the vacuolar cargo signal no longer declined during the early-to-late transition.
source: In the absence of Vps10, the vacuolar cargo signal no longer declined during the early-to-late transition (Figure 4—video 2, Figure 4D–F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4 and associated videos.

claim: vps10∆ cells displayed a transient increase in the cargo signal during the early-to-late transition, likely due to AP-1-dependent recycling from older cisternae.
source: Instead, vps10∆ cells actually displayed a transient increase in the cargo signal during the early-to-late transition, likely due to AP-1-dependent recycling from older cisternae as previously shown for the fluorescent secretory cargo (Casler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data with an interpretation based on prior work.

claim: In wild-type cells, the vacuolar cargo begins to exit the Golgi in a Vps10-dependent manner around the time of the early-to-late transition.
source: These data indicate that in wild-type cells, the vacuolar cargo begins to exit the Golgi in a Vps10-dependent manner around the time of the early-to-late transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of wild-type and vps10∆ cells.

claim: Gga2 consistently showed arrival and departure kinetics nearly identical to those of Sec7.
source: Gga2 consistently showed arrival and departure kinetics nearly identical to those of Sec7, whereas Apl2 consistently arrived ~20–40 s later and departed ~10–15 s later than Gga2 and Sec7 (Figure 5—video 1, Figure 5A,B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5 and associated videos.

claim: Apl2 consistently arrived ~20–40 s later and departed ~10–15 s later than Gga2 and Sec7.
source: Gga2 consistently showed arrival and departure kinetics nearly identical to those of Sec7, whereas Apl2 consistently arrived ~20–40 s later and departed ~10–15 s later than Gga2 and Sec7 (Figure 5—video 1, Figure 5A,B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5 and associated videos.

claim: The first appearance of Gga2 occurred at about the same time that the vacuolar cargo signal started to decline.
source: Indeed, when the vacuolar cargo was visualized in maturing cisternae together with the early Golgi marker GFP-Vrg4 and with Gga2-HaloTag, the first appearance of Gga2 occurred at about the same time that the vacuolar cargo signal started to decline (Figure 5—video 2, Figure 5C,D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5 and associated videos.

claim: The cargo signal sometimes began to drop a short time before Gga2 was visible at the Golgi.
source: Interestingly, the cargo signal sometimes began to drop a short time before Gga2 was visible at the Golgi.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: When GGAs are first recruited, they are immediately packaged into vesicles that transport vacuolar cargoes from the Golgi, so the pool of Golgi-associated Gga2 initially remains low.
source: A potential explanation is that when GGAs are first recruited, they are immediately packaged into vesicles that transport vacuolar cargoes from the Golgi, so the pool of Golgi-associated Gga2 initially remains low.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation.

claim: In the apl4∆ strain, the vacuolar cargo signal began to decline during the early-to-late transition of Golgi maturation in a manner indistinguishable from that seen in wild-type cells.
source: In the apl4∆ strain, the vacuolar cargo signal began to decline during the early-to-late transition of Golgi maturation in a manner indistinguishable from that seen in wild-type cells (Figure 6—video 1, Figure 6A–C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6 and associated videos.

claim: In the gga1∆ gga2∆ strain, the vacuolar cargo persisted during the early-to-late transition.
source: Strikingly, in the gga1∆ gga2∆ strain, the vacuolar cargo persisted during the early-to-late transition (Figure 6—video 2, Figure 6D–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6 and associated videos.

claim: In most of the events analyzed for the gga1∆ gga2∆ strain, the vacuolar cargo could be detected within the cisterna until the Sec7 signal disappeared or even afterwards.
source: In most of the events analyzed for the gga1∆ gga2∆ strain, the vacuolar cargo could be detected within the cisterna until the Sec7 signal disappeared or even afterwards (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6 and associated figure supplements.

claim: The gga1∆ gga2∆ strain displayed somewhat altered Vrg4 and Sec7 maturation kinetics, as indicated by abnormally shallow slopes for the arrival and departure curves of the Golgi markers.
source: A caveat is that the gga1∆ gga2∆ strain displayed somewhat altered Vrg4 and Sec7 maturation kinetics, as indicated by abnormally shallow slopes for the arrival and departure curves of the Golgi markers (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: GGAs are needed for the vacuolar cargo to exit the Golgi.
source: Nevertheless, maturation events could be readily identified in the gga1∆ gga2∆ strain, and the results strongly suggest that GGAs are needed for the vacuolar cargo to exit the Golgi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of wild-type and gga1∆ gga2∆ cells.

claim: Loss of GGAs causes the vacuolar cargo to be secreted.
source: As a further test of this interpretation, we hypothesized that loss of GGAs would cause the vacuolar cargo to be secreted, as is true for native CPY (Dell'Angelica et al., 2000; Hirst et al., 2000; Zhdankina et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior studies of CPY secretion.

claim: Secreted cargo was consistently observed with the vps10∆ and gga1∆ gga2∆ strains but not with the wild-type or apl4∆ strains.
source: Secreted cargo was consistently observed with the vps10∆ and gga1∆ gga2∆ strains but not with the wild-type or apl4∆ strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The wild-type, apl4∆, and apm3∆ strains all showed similar amounts of vacuolar cargo, while the vps10∆ and gga1∆ gga2∆ strains showed very little vacuolar cargo.
source: The wild-type, apl4∆, and apm3∆ strains all showed similar amounts of vacuolar cargo, while the vps10∆ and gga1∆ gga2∆ strains showed very little vacuolar cargo (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The vacuolar cargo is sorted to PVE compartments after the early-to-late Golgi transition, with the aid of Vps10 and GGAs but with no significant contribution from AP-1.
source: The combined results indicate that the vacuolar cargo is sorted to PVE compartments after the early-to-late Golgi transition, with the aid of Vps10 and GGAs but with no significant contribution from AP-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and kinetic analyses.

claim: Cargo fluorescence moved from PVE compartments to the vacuole.
source: As previously documented (Day et al., 2018), the Vps8-GFP-labeled PVE compartments were persistent structures. Meanwhile, cargo fluorescence moved from PVE compartments to the vacuole.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: During the majority of a typical time course, the fluorescence in a PVE compartment gradually declined, and this decrease was matched by a gradual increase of fluorescence in the vacuole.
source: During the majority of a typical time course, the fluorescence in a PVE compartment gradually declined, and this decrease was matched by a gradual increase of fluorescence in the vacuole (Figure 7—video 1 and Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7 and associated videos.

claim: Occasionally, a discrete event rapidly transferred a substantial fraction of the cargo fluorescence to the vacuole.
source: Occasionally, a discrete event rapidly transferred a substantial fraction of the cargo fluorescence to the vacuole (Figure 7—video 2 and Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7 and associated videos.

claim: The punctate PVE compartments marked with Vps8-GFP were never seen to disappear.
source: Although the Vps8-GFP signal varied, and sometimes dropped after a discrete event, the punctate PVE compartments marked with Vps8-GFP were never seen to disappear.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: The vacuolar cargo moves from long-lived PVE compartments to the vacuole by a series of kiss-and-run events that are frequently small and sometimes large.
source: Our interpretation is that the vacuolar cargo moves from long-lived PVE compartments to the vacuole by a series of kiss-and-run events that are frequently small and sometimes large.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the microscopy data.

claim: The Mup1 cargo moved from PVE compartments to the vacuole, sometimes gradually and sometimes in discrete bursts.
source: Once again, apparent kiss-and-run transfer was readily observed. The Mup1 cargo moved from PVE compartments to the vacuole, sometimes gradually and sometimes in discrete bursts (Figure 8—video 1 and Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8 and associated videos.

claim: Rarely, a dramatic event results in transfer of virtually all of the Mup1 in a single burst.
source: Rarely, a dramatic event results in transfer of virtually all of the Mup1 in a single burst (Figure 8—video 2 and Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8 and associated videos.

claim: Complete loss of Vps8 was never observed as would be expected for a full fusion event.
source: We never observed complete loss of Vps8 as would be expected for a full fusion event, although a subset of the larger discrete events led to substantial reduction of the Vps8 signal (Figure 8—video 3 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data shown in Figure 8 and associated videos.

claim: For both the vacuolar cargo and Mup1, gradual transfer to the vacuole was punctuated, about once every 5 min on average, by bursts in which > 15% of the remaining cargo moved to the vacuole.
source: For both the vacuolar cargo and Mup1, quantification revealed that gradual transfer to the vacuole was punctuated, about once every 5 min on average, by bursts in which > 15% of the remaining cargo moved to the vacuole.
evidence: This is based on quantification of microscopy data.

claim: The average amount of remaining cargo transferred during a burst was ~35–40%.
source: The average amount of remaining cargo transferred during a burst was ~35–40%.
evidence: This is based on quantification of microscopy data.

claim: Individual PVE compartments differed greatly in the total fraction of the cargo that was transferred in bursts, but on average this number was ~75%.
source: Individual PVE compartments differed greatly in the total fraction of the cargo that was transferred in bursts, but on average this number was ~75%.
evidence: This is based on quantification of microscopy data.

claim: The results favor a PVE-to-vacuole traffic mechanism involving repeated kiss-and-run events of varying size.
source: These results favor a PVE-to-vacuole traffic mechanism involving repeated kiss-and-run events of varying size.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantification of cargo transfer events.

claim: Compared to CPY, which is monomeric, the vacuolar cargo is a tetramer and thus contains four copies of the Vps10 recognition signal.
source: Compared to CPY, which is monomeric (Endrizzi et al., 1994), our vacuolar cargo is a tetramer and thus contains four copies of the Vps10 recognition signal.
evidence: This is a description of the structural difference between the artificial cargo and native CPY, with a citation.

claim: Vps10 has a quality control domain that recognizes the fluorescent protein component of the cargo.
source: Moreover, Vps10 has a quality control domain that recognizes the fluorescent protein component of the cargo (Casler et al., 2019; Fitzgerald and Glick, 2014), so there are multiple points of interaction between Vps10 and the artificial vacuolar cargo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The vacuolar cargo might dissociate from Vps10 more slowly than CPY dissociates, leading to slower PVE-to-vacuole delivery.
source: A consequence is that our vacuolar cargo might dissociate from Vps10 more slowly than CPY dissociates, leading to slower PVE-to-vacuole delivery.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential caveat of the artificial cargo system.

claim: The new insight is that departure of the vacuolar cargo from the Golgi begins relatively early, about halfway through the time course of cisternal maturation.
source: The new insight is that departure of the vacuolar cargo from the Golgi begins relatively early, about halfway through the time course of cisternal maturation (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, with reference to a figure.

claim: In a typical cultured mammalian cell, the early Golgi consists of about six cisternae whereas the clathrin-labeled TGN is a single cisterna.
source: In a typical cultured mammalian cell, the early Golgi consists of about six cisternae whereas the clathrin-labeled TGN is a single cisterna (Ladinsky et al., 1999; Mogelsvang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies of mammalian Golgi.

claim: In yeast, the ratio is different because the clathrin-labeled late Golgi/TGN stage occupies about half of the maturation time course.
source: In yeast, the ratio is different because the clathrin-labeled late Golgi/TGN stage occupies about half of the maturation time course (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is based on the kinetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In both cell types, GGA-dependent transport occurs during the TGN stage, but the yeast system has allowed us to define a first TGN sub-stage marked by GGA activity followed by a second TGN sub-stage marked by AP-1 activity.
source: In both cell types, GGA-dependent transport occurs during the TGN stage, but the yeast system has allowed us to define a first TGN sub-stage marked by GGA activity followed by a second TGN sub-stage marked by AP-1 activity (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Mammalian TGN structures probably undergo a similar kinetic evolution because the interactions of clathrin adaptors at the mammalian TGN resemble those at the yeast TGN.
source: Mammalian TGN structures probably undergo a similar kinetic evolution because the interactions of clathrin adaptors at the mammalian TGN resemble those at the yeast TGN (Daboussi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on similarities between yeast and mammalian systems, with a citation.

claim: During traffic to either yeast PVE compartments or mammalian late endosomes, GGA-dependent export from the TGN begins prior to secretory vesicle formation and AP-1-dependent intra-Golgi recycling.
source: A proposed unified view is that during traffic to either yeast PVE compartments or mammalian late endosomes, GGA-dependent export from the TGN begins prior to secretory vesicle formation and AP-1-dependent intra-Golgi recycling (Pantazopoulou and Glick, 2019).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings, with a citation.

claim: Mammalian cells can employ kiss-and-run fusion to exchange material between lysosomes and late endosomes.
source: This model seemed plausible because mammalian cells can employ kiss-and-run fusion to exchange material between lysosomes and late endosomes (Bright et al., 2016; Bright et al., 2005; Saffi and Botelho, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in mammalian cells.

claim: An electron tomographic reconstruction shows tubular membrane connections between PVE compartments and the vacuole.
source: Notably, an electron tomographic reconstruction carried out by the Odorizzi group (McNatt et al., 2007), reprinted here as Figure 8—figure supplement 2, shows tubular membrane connections between PVE compartments and the vacuole.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior electron microscopy study and an image shown in the manuscript.

claim: The results suggest that tubular connections between PVE compartments and the vacuole should be common.
source: Our results suggest that such tubular connections should be common, so their prevalence could be quantified in future morphological studies.
evidence: This is an inference from the kiss-and-run model proposed by the authors.

claim: PVE compartments were sometimes observed to form clusters.
source: A separate electron tomographic analysis highlighted a possible complication—PVE compartments were sometimes observed to form clusters (Adell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior electron microscopy study.

claim: If a single PVE compartment in a cluster fused completely with the vacuole, the fluorescence from the remaining PVE compartments in the cluster would persist, yielding a false impression of kiss-and-run fusion.
source: If a single PVE compartment in a cluster fused completely with the vacuole, the fluorescence from the remaining PVE compartments in the cluster would persist, yielding a false impression of kiss-and-run fusion.
evidence: This is a potential alternative explanation for the observations.

claim: Some PVE compartments are presumably solitary and yet we have never seen one disappear by fusing completely with the vacuole.
source: Although we cannot rule out this scenario, it seems unlikely, because some PVE compartments are presumably solitary and yet we have never seen one disappear by fusing completely with the vacuole.
evidence: This is an argument against the alternative explanation, based on the authors' observations.

claim: If kiss-and-run transfer occurs between PVE compartments and the vacuole, the transient continuities between these organelles might permit exchange of freely diffusing transmembrane proteins.
source: If kiss-and-run transfer occurs between PVE compartments and the vacuole, the transient continuities between these organelles might permit exchange of freely diffusing transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation about a consequence of the kiss-and-run model.

claim: A mutant carboxypeptidase S precursor that cannot be internalized moves from the limiting membranes of PVE compartments to the vacuole membrane.
source: For example, the transmembrane precursor to the vacuolar hydrolase carboxypeptidase S is normally internalized into intraluminal vesicles of PVE compartments, but a mutant carboxypeptidase S precursor that cannot be internalized moves from the limiting membranes of PVE compartments to the vacuole membrane (Katzmann et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Overexpressed Vps10 and Pep12 reach the vacuole membrane.
source: Although other transmembrane proteins such as Vps10 and the SNARE protein Pep12 normally reside in PVE compartments and not in the vacuole membrane, overexpressed Vps10 and Pep12 do reach the vacuole membrane (Black and Pelham, 2000; Cereghino et al., 1995; Chi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During transient fusions of PVE compartments with the vacuole, saturable interactions with the trafficking machinery retain proteins such as Vps10 and Pep12 in the PVE compartments.
source: It seems plausible that during transient fusions of PVE compartments with the vacuole, saturable interactions with the trafficking machinery retain proteins such as Vps10 and Pep12 in the PVE compartments.
evidence: This is a speculation about a mechanism that could explain the observations.

claim: The kiss-and-run model can explain how some transmembrane PVE proteins reach the vacuole while others do not, whereas this phenomenon would be hard to understand if PVE compartments fused completely with the vacuole.
source: Hence, the kiss-and-run model can explain how some transmembrane PVE proteins reach the vacuole while others do not, whereas this phenomenon would be hard to understand if PVE compartments fused completely with the vacuole.
evidence: This is an argument in favor of the kiss-and-run model based on logical inference.

claim: Cargo transfer from PVE compartments to the vacuole is slow relative to other membrane traffic steps in budding yeast.
source: Cargo transfer from PVE compartments to the vacuole is slow relative to other membrane traffic steps in budding yeast.
evidence: This is a summary of the kinetic findings.

claim: Kinetics of traffic to the vacuole have been measured by pulse-chase experiments that rely on the maturation of CPY by vacuolar proteases, but those results may be misleading because kiss-and-run fusion could result in some vacuolar proteases being present and active in PVE compartments.
source: Historically, kinetics of traffic to the vacuole have been measured by pulse-chase experiments that rely on the maturation of CPY by vacuolar proteases (Stevens et al., 1982; Vida et al., 1993), but those results may be misleading because kiss-and-run fusion could result in some vacuolar proteases being present and active in PVE compartments (Bright et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a critique of prior methods based on the kiss-and-run model, with citations.

claim: As judged by fluorescence microscopy, PVE-to-vacuole transfer often requires 30 min or more to reach completion.
source: As judged by fluorescence microscopy, PVE-to-vacuole transfer often requires 30 min or more to reach completion.
evidence: This is based on the kinetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transit from the ER to the PVE along the biosynthetic pathway or from the plasma membrane to the PVE along the endocytic pathway is largely complete within 10 min.
source: By comparison, transit from the ER to the PVE along the biosynthetic pathway or from the plasma membrane to the PVE along the endocytic pathway is largely complete within 10 min (Casler et al., 2019; Day et al., 2018; Losev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A possible reason for PVE-to-vacuole traffic being rate-limiting is that the cell has the option to 'change its mind' by recycling membrane proteins from the PVE instead of degrading them.
source: A possible reason for PVE-to-vacuole traffic being rate-limiting is that the cell has the option to 'change its mind' by recycling membrane proteins from the PVE instead of degrading them (Ma and Burd, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological significance of the slow kinetics, with a citation.

claim: The AP-3-driven pathway of direct Golgi-to-vacuole traffic offers an alternative for rapid delivery of membrane proteins to the vacuole.
source: Meanwhile, the AP-3-driven pathway of direct Golgi-to-vacuole traffic offers an alternative for rapid delivery of membrane proteins to the vacuole (Odorizzi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.
